## Abstract

Predicting the next demand event requires estimating both its timing and its quantity from an irregular history. We present TitanTPP, a compact architecture that combines causal gap–quantity encoding with a bottleneck history correction between attention blocks. The correction relates current and immediately preceding contextual states, while learned static banks provide additional context without online parameter updates. We compare TitanTPP with six temporal point process encoders under a shared input, prediction-head, loss, and checkpoint-selection protocol. Three-seed validation comparisons cover Taxi, Intermittent, RAF, and Instacart. TitanTPP reduces mean quantity RMSE by 15.85% on Taxi and 34.39% on Intermittent relative to the strongest external comparator on each dataset, with lower MAE and RMSE than all six comparators in every seed on these two datasets. On RAF, a small RMSE advantage accompanies higher MAE than the best external comparator. Instacart exhibits small MAE gains over S2P2 and AttNHP but higher RMSE, with larger errors concentrated in the higher-quantity strata. Duration-likelihood rankings differ from quantity-error rankings. In matched Taxi and Intermittent batch measurements, the Titans-MAC adapter requires 5.58–5.74 times TitanTPP’s training-step compute time, while TitanTPP reduces peak allocated training memory by approximately 75.5%. Its evaluation memory allocation is higher. These findings support compact history correction for quantity prediction, with the strongest accuracy gains on Taxi and Intermittent.

## 8. Conclusion

TitanTPP integrates a bottleneck correction of adjacent contextual states into a causal event encoder. Persistent vectors and static prototype retrieval complement this history path, connecting observed gaps and quantities to next-event prediction with fixed parameters during inference. The architecture provides a compact way to incorporate recent-event relationships between contextual encoding stages.

The four-dataset, three-seed validation study identifies the strongest quantity gains on Taxi and Intermittent. Under the common-head protocol, TitanTPP reduces mean RMSE by 15.85% and 34.39%, respectively, relative to the best external comparator, and reduces both MAE and RMSE in all paired seed comparisons on these datasets. RAF yields a small RMSE advantage with an MAE trade-off. On Instacart, the small MAE gains over S2P2 and AttNHP accompany higher RMSE in every paired seed, with high-quantity errors outweighing gains on smaller quantities. Duration likelihood follows a different ranking. The Instacart error breakdown points to high-quantity prediction as a specific target for further architectural study.

Matched batch measurements complement the accuracy results with lower training-step compute time and peak allocated training memory than the Titans-MAC adapter. Evaluation batches are also faster, although their memory allocation is higher. Together, the experiments support compact history correction as a practical design for next-event quantity prediction whose accuracy gains depend on the demand setting. Independent evaluation with frozen model choices and further analysis of high-quantity errors are the next steps toward assessing its reliability beyond the validation partitions used in development.
